paragraphs: Using fewer numerical levels for neural network activations can help fit models into resource-constrained environments. This paper studies how that reduction in precision affects the passage of signals through a network at initialization. Its focus is the relationship between activation quantization and the depth that a network can support.

The authors apply mean field techniques to analyze signal propagation and derive initialization schemes that maximize it for quantized activations. This connects the choice of numerical precision with the choice of initial network parameters. They also suggest why preserving signals in this way could help generalization, rather than establishing that benefit as an unconditional result.

The analysis produces an implicit equation connecting the number of activation levels, N, to the maximal trainable depth, L_max. Numerically solving that equation gives the asymptotic relationship L_max proportional to N raised to 1.82. Within this theoretical account, adding quantization levels permits greater depth, making precision and model capacity linked design choices.
neurips-2019-a-mean-field-theory-of-quan.tldr: A mean field analysis links activation precision to trainable network depth and derives initialization schemes that improve signal propagation.

paragraphs: Private data analysis faces a practical question: who must users trust with their information? In the global model of differential privacy, users trust the collector, allowing strong privacy guarantees with relatively small output errors. In the local model, users randomize their information before sharing it because they do not trust that collector.

The paper argues that the local model's requirements restrict its usefulness for several important applications. It proposes a framework based on trusted processors and introduces a privacy definition called Oblivious Differential Privacy. The intended benefit is to combine desirable properties of the global and local models by making trusted processing part of the design.

The contribution also includes algorithms that bring together ideas from streaming computation, oblivious algorithms, and differential privacy. This makes the work an algorithmic framework as well as a proposed privacy definition. Its central significance is a different arrangement of trust for private analysis: the stated framework relies on trusted processors to pursue the benefits of both established models.
neurips-2019-an-algorithmic-framework-fo.tldr: The paper introduces Oblivious Differential Privacy and a trusted-processor framework intended to combine benefits of global and local privacy models.

paragraphs: DISN reconstructs a detailed three-dimensional shape from a single image. It represents the shape through a signed distance field, which describes the surface through distance predictions at points in space. Predicting this underlying field allows the network to generate a three-dimensional mesh from the two-dimensional input.

The central design combines information about the whole image with information tied to individual spatial points. For each three-dimensional point, DISN predicts where it projects onto the image and extracts features from that location. These local features complement the global image representation, helping the model connect fine visual evidence to the corresponding parts of the reconstructed shape.

The authors report that combining these feature sources substantially improves distance-field accuracy, especially in detailed regions. They emphasize the capture of holes and thin structures, and report leading reconstruction performance across several shape categories using synthetic and real images. The findings support the value of connecting local image evidence to spatial queries when reconstructing fine geometry from one view.
neurips-2019-disn-deep-implicit-surface-.tldr: DISN combines global image features with point-specific local features to reconstruct detailed 3D surfaces from a single image.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a linear decision boundary when examples have noisy labels and the input distribution is arbitrary. The labels originate from an unknown halfspace and are corrupted under the Massart noise model, with noise rate eta below one half. The learner aims to predict the observed labels with low misclassification error.

The authors give an algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the input dimension and inverse error tolerance. Its error is at most eta plus epsilon, connecting achievable prediction quality to the assumed noise bound. The distribution-independent requirement matters because the algorithm does not need the unlabeled examples to follow a particular distribution.

This establishes efficient learning in a setting where even a weak learner had not previously been known, including for the simpler class of disjunctions. The paper also presents evidence that a stronger error guarantee may be computationally difficult. That evidence qualifies the result's frontier without establishing an unconditional impossibility of improving it.
neurips-2019-distribution-independent-pa.tldr: The paper gives an efficient distribution-independent learner for halfspaces with Massart noise, achieving error at most the noise bound plus epsilon.

paragraphs: Online learning can require repeatedly returning to options that were useful earlier. This paper develops a general framework for long-term memory guarantees, comparing a learner with sequences that switch among experts while reusing a limited number of distinct experts. The approach reduces this problem to obtaining conventional switching-regret guarantees.

For K actions and T rounds, the framework yields regret of order sqrt(T(S ln T + n ln K)), against sequences with S minus one switches among n distinct experts. The bound separately tracks switching and the number of different experts used. With particular adaptive algorithms plugged into the framework, the authors also obtain guarantees suited to both stochastic and adversarial environments simultaneously.

The paper extends its investigation to sparse multi-armed bandits, establishing both positive and negative results for long-term memory. A related lower bound shows that sparse losses do not improve worst-case contextual-bandit regret. This distinguishes the contextual setting from the non-contextual one and identifies a boundary on the usefulness of sparsity.
neurips-2019-equipping-experts-bandits-w.tldr: A general reduction gives online learners long-term memory guarantees that account for both expert switching and reuse.

paragraphs: Protein learning faces expensive supervised labels and inconsistent evaluation across studies. TAPE addresses the evaluation problem with five biologically relevant tasks spanning different areas of protein biology. The authors construct training, validation, and test splits intended to assess generalization that matters for real biological applications.

The benchmark compares several approaches to semi-supervised protein representation learning, including recent methods and established sequence-learning techniques. Its shared tasks and evaluation structure make it possible to examine whether learned representations transfer usefully across different biological problems. This places emphasis on what a representation supports after pretraining, rather than treating pretraining itself as sufficient evidence of usefulness.

Self-supervised pretraining helps almost all evaluated models across all tasks, with performance more than doubling in some cases. Nevertheless, pretrained features remain behind leading non-neural features in several comparisons. These findings show both the value of pretraining and room for better biological representations. The released data and code provide a common basis for investigating that gap.
neurips-2019-evaluating-protein-transfer.tldr: TAPE standardizes protein transfer-learning evaluation and finds broad benefits from pretraining alongside persistent gaps against non-neural features.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Matrix Krasulina, an algorithm for learning a principal subspace from data arriving online. Principal component analysis seeks a compact set of directions that captures the data's main variation. The authors extend the classic vector-based Krasulina method to a matrix formulation that handles multiple principal directions.

The central finding is that the algorithm adapts naturally to data with low-rank structure. Theoretical analysis and empirical results show exponential convergence toward the ground-truth principal subspace in the intrinsically low-rank setting. This ties the speed of learning to the structure of the data, rather than describing exponential convergence as a guarantee for every possible input distribution.

The result matters because other acceleration efforts add a variance-reduction step requiring time proportional to the number of examples. Here, the stated fast convergence is achieved by a genuinely online stochastic-gradient variant without that additional step. For the setting studied, this shows that exploiting low-rank structure can make such variance reduction unnecessary for exponential convergence.
neurips-2019-exponentially-convergent-st.tldr: Matrix Krasulina achieves exponential convergence for online principal-subspace learning on intrinsically low-rank data without an added variance-reduction step.

paragraphs: Video-to-video synthesis turns structured video inputs, such as poses or segmentation masks, into photorealistic video. Existing approaches described in this paper require many images of a target person or scene and generalize poorly to new targets. A model trained to render one person, for example, remains tied to that person's appearance.

The proposed framework learns to synthesize videos of previously unseen subjects or scenes using only a few target images at test time. Its key component generates network weights using an attention mechanism. This makes the example images part of how the model adapts its synthesis behavior to a new target.

The authors evaluate the framework against strong baselines on large-scale datasets covering dancing people, talking heads, and street scenes. They report that the results support its effectiveness in addressing both target-data requirements and limited generalization. The contribution is therefore a way to reuse a learned video-synthesis system across new appearances, with a few reference images supplying the target-specific information.
neurips-2019-few-shot-video-to-video-syn.tldr: An attention-based weight-generation module enables video synthesis for unseen subjects or scenes from a few example images.

paragraphs: A Gaussian process uses a covariance kernel to express relationships between inputs, so the kernel strongly shapes what the model can learn. This paper introduces functional kernel learning, which infers a distribution over kernel functions. The aim is to learn useful representations while retaining uncertainty about the kernel itself.

The method places a transformed Gaussian process over a spectral density, inducing a non-parametric distribution over kernels. This construction supports any stationary kernel and allows an interpretable prior to be specified directly over kernels. The authors use elliptical slice sampling for inference, describing it as particularly suitable for the strongly correlated priors involved in function-space modeling.

The approach is developed for irregularly sampled, large-scale, multi-task, and multidimensional data. Experiments report promising results in interpolation, extrapolation, and recovering kernels, without requiring elaborate initialization or manual intervention. The significance is that kernel learning becomes an uncertainty-aware inference problem, rather than requiring commitment to a single fixed covariance structure before analyzing the data.
neurips-2019-function-space-distribution.tldr: Functional kernel learning infers flexible distributions over stationary kernels while retaining uncertainty about their values.

paragraphs: Energy-based models offer a general approach to likelihood modeling, but training them has traditionally been difficult. This paper develops techniques for scaling training based on Markov chain Monte Carlo to continuous neural networks. The goal is to make this flexible modeling approach work on high-dimensional data.

The authors demonstrate the approach on two ImageNet resolutions, CIFAR-10, and robotic hand trajectories. They report better samples than other likelihood models and sample quality approaching contemporary generative adversarial networks, while covering all data modes. They also demonstrate compositional generation, reconstruction of corrupted images, and inpainting, highlighting several uses of the learned model beyond generating complete images.

Further results cover out-of-distribution classification, adversarially robust classification, continual online class learning, and long-term trajectory prediction. The authors report leading performance for out-of-distribution classification and continual online class learning, together with coherent predicted trajectories. Taken together, these stated findings present scalable energy-based training as a route to a broadly useful model across generation and prediction tasks.
neurips-2019-implicit-generation-and-mod.tldr: The paper scales MCMC-based energy-model training and demonstrates strong generation, reconstruction, classification, and trajectory-modeling capabilities.

paragraphs: This paper asks how difficult it is to learn a linear classifier when the returned classifier must itself be a halfspace. It studies points in the unit ball and compares prediction error with the best achievable margin error. The target guarantee allows a multiplicative approximation factor and an additional error tolerance.

The authors give algorithms and computational hardness results across approximation factors of at least one. For a factor of 1.01, their learner uses an optimal number of samples, proportional to 1/(epsilon squared times gamma squared). Its runtime is polynomial in dimension and inverse tolerance, multiplied by an exponential term whose exponent depends roughly on inverse margin squared.

The matching obstruction is conditional on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Under that assumption, any constant-factor proper learner needs nearly the same exponential dependence on inverse margin. Thus, for constant factors greater than one, the results largely characterize computational difficulty: efficient use of examples does not remove the steep runtime dependence on a small margin.
neurips-2019-nearly-tight-bounds-for-rob.tldr: Nearly matching algorithms and conditional hardness bounds characterize the cost of properly learning halfspaces relative to optimal margin error.

paragraphs: Mixup creates training examples by blending pairs of images and their labels. This paper examines how that training procedure affects confidence estimates, extending attention beyond classification accuracy. A well-calibrated classifier gives confidence scores that reliably reflect how often its predictions are actually correct.

Across multiple image architectures and datasets, including ImageNet, the authors find that mixup produces substantially better calibration than ordinary training. Their investigation also finds that mixing features alone does not provide the same benefit. Blending the labels, which softens the training targets, plays a significant role in making confidence more informative.

The authors additionally observe less overconfidence on inputs outside the training distribution and on random noise. They interpret these results as suggesting that hard training labels are a likely source of neural-network overconfidence, even for familiar kinds of input. This is an empirical explanation and recommendation: mixup appears useful when trustworthy predictive uncertainty matters, without implying that every confidence score becomes reliable.
neurips-2019-on-mixup-training-improved-.tldr: Mixup empirically improves confidence calibration and reduces overconfidence, with softened labels playing a significant role.

paragraphs: Personalized decision-making can involve both many possible actions and many descriptive features. This paper studies that combination in a stochastic contextual bandit with k actions and d features. Its concern is how the regret guarantee grows as those two dimensions become large.

The proposed REAL Bandit algorithm uses low-rank structure in the unknown parameter matrix, whose rows correspond to actions and whose columns correspond to features. If that matrix has rank r, the stated dependence of regret on these quantities is r squared times (k plus d). The authors contrast this with existing guarantees they identify as having polynomial dependence of degree at least two in k and d.

REAL Bandit draws on low-rank matrix estimation and introduces a row-enhancement procedure that sharpens estimates of individual parameter rows. This matters because the learner needs useful estimates for particular actions, not merely a global matrix estimate. The benefit of the stated scaling depends on rank, making shared low-dimensional structure central to the approach.
neurips-2019-personalizing-many-decision.tldr: REAL Bandit exploits low-rank parameter structure to improve regret scaling when both the action set and feature dimension are large.

paragraphs: Gibbs sampling supports learning and inference in graphical models, but processing a large graph can make each iteration expensive. Minibatching reduces that work by using a small random subset of the graph. This paper develops a minibatched method that pairs computational savings with guarantees about sampling behavior.

The proposed Poisson-minibatching Gibbs method introduces auxiliary variables as part of its sampling construction. The authors state that it produces unbiased samples and provide a theoretical guarantee on its convergence rate. These properties address separate concerns: retaining the intended sampling behavior and understanding how quickly the sampling process converges.

Compared with earlier minibatched Gibbs methods, the approach supports fast sampling in continuous state spaces and avoids a Metropolis-Hastings correction for discrete state spaces. The authors demonstrate effectiveness across multiple applications, comparing it with ordinary Gibbs sampling and previous minibatched approaches. The contribution is therefore both a sampling construction and an analysis supporting its use when large graphical models make full iterations costly.
neurips-2019-poisson-minibatching-for-gi.tldr: Poisson-minibatching makes Gibbs sampling cheaper while preserving unbiased sampling and providing a convergence-rate guarantee.

paragraphs: Goal-directed reinforcement learning becomes difficult when rewards are sparse: experience may provide little direct feedback about how to reach the requested goal. This paper introduces Policy Continuation with Hindsight Inverse Dynamics, or PCHID, to learn more effectively from that experience. Its starting point is hindsight experience replay.

PCHID learns through hindsight inverse dynamics in a self-imitation process that can be trained with supervised learning. The approach uses the agent's own experience as a basis for learning how to act. Policy Continuation extends this learning process to multi-step settings, connecting the hindsight-based training approach with tasks requiring sequences of actions.

The method can operate on its own or be combined with other on-policy and off-policy algorithms. On the two evaluated multi-goal tasks, GridWorld and FetchReach, the authors report substantial improvements in sample efficiency and final performance. These findings support hindsight-based self-imitation as a useful source of training information when successful goal-directed behavior is difficult to learn from sparse rewards alone.
neurips-2019-policy-continuation-with-hi.tldr: PCHID uses hindsight-based supervised self-imitation and multi-step policy continuation to improve learning on two sparse-reward goal tasks.

paragraphs: Understanding video requires connecting local appearance with interactions that unfold across space and time. This paper proposes a recurrent graph model for that purpose. It aims to represent both individual parts of a changing scene and higher-level relationships among its entities and objects.

The graph assigns neural networks to both nodes and edges. Nodes process features from local regions in space and time together with previous memory states. Edges process messages linking different locations, spatial scales, and past and present information. Repeated message passing allows information to travel throughout the graph and establish longer-range interactions.

Experiments and ablation studies show better complex-activity recognition than strong baselines and leading published methods, including leading performance on the Something-Something human-object interaction dataset. The authors describe the architecture as general enough to potentially support other spatiotemporal concepts and learning tasks. The demonstrated findings concern video activity recognition, where the graph's coordinated processing of appearance, memory, and interaction is directly relevant.
neurips-2019-recurrent-space-time-graph-.tldr: A recurrent graph exchanges information across space, scale, and time to improve recognition of complex video activities.

paragraphs: The secretary ranking problem asks an algorithm to place arriving elements into an ordering without revising earlier placements. Elements arrive in random order, and each decision uses only comparisons with elements already seen. Quality is measured by inversions: pairs whose assigned order disagrees with their true order.

For n elements and n available positions, the paper gives an algorithm with expected inversion count of order n raised to 3/2. It also proves a matching lower bound for any algorithm. Together, these results identify the optimal growth rate of ranking error under the stated information and irrevocability constraints.

The analysis connects the algorithm to linear probing in hashing, while the lower bound uses an anti-concentration result for a balls-and-bins sampling process. The authors also consider having more available positions than arriving elements and derive an improved bound through a connection with random binary trees. Thus, the work characterizes the standard setting and shows how additional placement space can improve the guarantee.
neurips-2019-secretary-ranking-with-mini.tldr: Matching bounds show that irrevocably ranking n randomly arriving elements into n positions requires expected inversion error of order n to the 3/2.

paragraphs: A seller setting prices can use customer history and product information, but cannot directly observe a customer's valuation. In this paper's setting, the seller sees only whether the transaction succeeds. The learning problem is therefore to choose revenue-generating prices while inferring willingness to pay from binary feedback.

The authors emphasize that the best price depends on detailed properties of the uncertainty left after accounting for contextual features. Their semi-parametric model combines regression parameters with a residual distribution that is modeled non-parametrically. Learning that distribution is part of the pricing problem, rather than treating contextual prediction alone as enough to determine the optimal action.

The proposed algorithm learns both components with regret growing at roughly the square root of the number of rounds, up to logarithmic factors. This is a cumulative performance guarantee while learning, connecting estimation of valuations with revenue decisions. A scalable implementation also performs well in the reported empirical tests, supporting the practical promise of the combined learning approach.
neurips-2019-semi-parametric-dynamic-con.tldr: The paper learns contextual valuation parameters and an unspecified residual distribution from purchase feedback with roughly square-root regret.

paragraphs: Tucker decomposition represents a multidimensional data array through latent factors. This paper develops a scalable way to infer those factors by processing one smaller subtensor at a time. The approach makes the update process operate on pieces of the data rather than requiring each update to handle the entire tensor.

Its main mechanism combines recursive gradient calculations with cyclic updates of the factors. Each factor update uses only one gradient-descent step. The authors also introduce a version using inexact gradients to improve computational efficiency further, giving two related algorithms for the same decomposition problem.

Both algorithms have theoretical guarantees for convergence and convergence rate under conditions described as mild. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the claimed scalability. The authors additionally state that the methods can readily accommodate common constraints such as non-negativity. The work therefore connects small incremental updates with convergence analysis and practical decomposition settings, including cases where the latent factors must satisfy additional requirements.
neurips-2019-singleshot-a-scalable-tucke.tldr: Singleshot scales Tucker decomposition through subtensor processing and single-step factor updates, with conditional convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Embedding layers can contain a large share of a neural network's parameters, making them an important target for regularization. This paper proposes stochastically shared embeddings, or SSE, as a data-driven way to constrain their learning. The method randomly transitions between embeddings during stochastic gradient descent.

The authors develop two versions. SSE-Graph uses a knowledge graph relating embeddings, while SSE-SE requires no prior information. Both fit into existing stochastic-gradient training with minor modifications. This makes the approach applicable within large neural-network training procedures without requiring an entirely separate optimization method.

The paper supplies theoretical guarantees and evaluates SSE on six tasks, ranging from recommender systems with simple networks to language models using transformers and BERT. The authors find that SSE can reduce overfitting further when combined with weight decay and dropout, often improving generalization. The empirical message is that regularizing how embeddings are used during training can complement established regularizers across the tested tasks and architectures.
neurips-2019-stochastic-shared-embedding.tldr: Stochastically shared embeddings regularize embedding layers through random transitions during training and can complement dropout and weight decay.

paragraphs: This paper examines what it means for an agent's representation of its environment to be disentangled. A precise definition matters for the broader aim of building autonomous agents that learn efficiently from data. The authors work within a symmetry-based definition that characterizes environmental structure using group theory.

Their central question is whether static observations provide an adequate basis for learning representations under that definition. Building on the earlier framework, they make theoretical and empirical observations that lead them to argue that agents need to interact with their environments to discover the relevant symmetries. Interaction therefore becomes part of how the agent learns the structure its representation is intended to capture.

The contribution concerns the information needed for symmetry-based disentangled learning, as well as the definition itself. Its conclusion is specifically framed around that approach to disentanglement. The authors provide reproducible experiments and code to support examination of their argument, linking the conceptual claim about interaction with empirical investigation.
neurips-2019-symmetry-based-disentangled.tldr: The authors argue, using theoretical and empirical observations, that symmetry-based disentangled learning requires interaction with the environment.

paragraphs: Injecting noise into a neural network at prediction time has shown practical promise against adversarial attacks. This paper investigates the theoretical basis for that strategy. It focuses on randomized inference and asks how the amount and form of randomization relate to robustness.

The first contribution establishes a relationship between randomization rate and resistance to adversarial attacks. The result applies to a general family of exponential distributions, extending and bringing together earlier approaches. This gives a broader theoretical account of noise-based defenses rather than an explanation tied to only one particular noise choice.

The second contribution is a new upper bound on the adversarial risk gap for randomized neural networks. Together, the two results provide ways to reason about the robustness consequences of inference-time noise. Experiments support the theoretical claims. The paper's contribution is a mathematical explanation and supporting evidence for this family of techniques, with claims expressed through relationships and bounds rather than an assertion of immunity to attacks.
neurips-2019-theoretical-evidence-for-ad.tldr: The paper relates inference-time randomization to adversarial robustness and derives a new upper bound on randomized networks' adversarial risk gap.

paragraphs: This paper studies choosing assortments of items over time to maximize cumulative revenue. The learner observes which offered item a user selects. Choices follow a multinomial logistic model, and each item's utility depends on changing contextual information about both the item and the user.

The authors propose two Thompson sampling algorithms. The first maintains a posterior over the unknown parameter and achieves Bayesian regret of roughly d times the square root of T, ignoring logarithmic factors. Its worst-case computational cost can be high when the prior is non-conjugate, motivating the second approach.

The second algorithm approximates the posterior with a Gaussian distribution and introduces an optimistic sampling procedure. Its worst-case frequentist regret is roughly d to the 3/2 times the square root of T, again up to logarithmic factors. These bounds use different notions of regret, so they describe distinct guarantees. Numerical experiments find practical behavior consistent with the theory, supporting both approaches to learning from contextual assortment choices.
neurips-2019-thompson-sampling-for-multi.tldr: Two Thompson sampling methods provide Bayesian and frequentist regret guarantees for contextual assortment selection under multinomial-logit choices.

paragraphs: Temporal convolutional networks offer computational advantages for sequence modeling, raising the question of what kinds of sequential behavior they can represent. This paper studies that question through input-output maps: rules that turn an input sequence into an output sequence. Its focus is systems with limited long-term temporal dependence.

The authors prove that temporal convolutional networks can approximate a broad class of maps with approximately finite memory to any desired error tolerance. The memory condition is central to the result. For systems with limited long-term dependencies, the paper describes convolutional and recurrent networks as having essentially equivalent approximation capability.

The analysis also gives quantitative approximation rates for deep networks with ReLU activations. These rates relate accuracy to network width, depth, and the continuity properties of the target map. The authors apply the results to systems admitting finite-dimensional state-space descriptions, connecting the theory to recurrent models. This provides both an existence result and a more detailed account of how network size relates to approximation.
neurips-2019-universal-approximation-of-.tldr: Temporal convolutional networks can approximate a broad class of approximately finite-memory systems, with rates tied to architecture and target continuity.

paragraphs: This paper questions how the apparent conflict between fairness and accuracy is evaluated. Its concern is that researchers may recognize biased labels when designing a fair model, then evaluate accuracy as though those labels were unbiased. Such a mismatch can affect what the measured trade-off means.

The authors investigate controlled settings with different amounts and types of bias. Under assumptions they describe as reasonable, they find that the tension disappears when evaluation accounts for these phenomena. Their results also support the possibility that fairness and accuracy can align, rather than implying that they always improve together.

The paper then explores using fairness requirements on predictions to learn from large amounts of unlabeled data. It applies ideas such as posterior regularization and generalized expectation in this semi-supervised setting. The reported results improve both fairness and accuracy and show advantages over existing in-processing methods affected by training-set selection bias. The contribution connects more consistent evaluation with a practical opportunity to use fairness as learning guidance.
neurips-2019-unlocking-fairness-a-trade-.tldr: Accounting for evaluation bias can remove an apparent fairness–accuracy trade-off, and fairness-guided semi-supervision improves both in the studied settings.
